title: That leopard seal scene still haunts me tbh #broadway #happyfeet #ani...
transcript: Alright, here's my pitch for the Broadway musical version of Happy Feet. Right off the bat, big question is like, what do you do about the Penguins? And I think that the penguins are not puppets. with how much time we spend with them as the central focus of the narrative and how much like the dancing is important to the narrative, I don't think they're puppets. I think we're leaning more in like a Lion King, SpongeBob kind of approach where they're humans in costumes that are meant to evoke and suggest that they are penguins. But then the really interesting question that comes is like, what do you do about the humans? Cause there are sections of the movie Happy Feet that very pivotally feature humans. And they made the cool choice in the movie to have those be live action while the rest of it was animated. And so my idea is, what if in the musical the humans are puppets? Cause that leads into how the penguins talk about them as like these strange, mysterious alien creatures. I guess you could also kind of carry over what they did in the movie and have the the humans be like projection video so that it still feels like there's that divide. By the way, I know a lot of people are gonna roll their eyes and be like, oh my god, another movie to musical adaptation. But like, I'm kinda down with this cause the Story is literally about expressing yourself through song and dance in a very deep and primal way. And lest we forget that this is not just some like, ordinary kids movie. Like this movie is dark and it's weird. And I'm excited that Michael Arden is directing it because I think he is a really smart and talented director. But I do hope that he is able to kind of find a way to replicate that weirdness that he leans into that a little more than maybe he usually does. Or rather, I would say not replicate the weirdness, but like find his own version of it that feels in his artistic voice. Cause I think that's where a lot of movie to musical adaptations go wrong. Like you can't take Baz Luhrmann or Hayao Miyazaki or George Miller in this case, out of their project without replacing that vision with something that feels just as distinct. I mean, you can, but you know…
